info.description:
SignalForge is an enterprise incident command centre. Any application is
onboarded through the public contracts in `signalforge/contracts/`; nothing in
this API names a vendor or an application.

**Authentication.** Human callers present a bearer access token from
`/auth/signup`, `/auth/login` or `/auth/refresh` (15 minutes, refreshed by a
rotating refresh token). Sending applications present an *ingest key*: a bearer
token plus an HMAC-SHA256 over `"<unix seconds>.<raw body>"` inside a 300-second
replay window. Every operation states which it wants, and which permission from
the roles matrix it requires, in the `x-signalforge-*` fields.

**Errors** are mapped once, in `signalforge/api/errors.py`: 401 authentication,
403 permission denied (with `permission` and `reason`), 404 not found, 409
conflict, 413 body too large, 422 domain validation *and* every policy-floor
refusal, 429 rate limited with `Retry-After`, 502 an integrated system failed,
504 an integrated system did not answer in time - which means the outcome is
unknown, not failed.

**Prose, decisions and the event catalogue** live in `docs/11-api-spec.md`;
this document is generated from the running application by
`scripts/gen_openapi.py` and is the same document `GET /openapi.json` serves.
info.title: SignalForge API

The policy in force, what it means for every published action, and the
immutable floor above which it sits.

`locked` on a row is the domain's answer, not the browser's: the six

post.description:
Write a new policy version.

A document that contradicts the platform safety floor is refused with 422
*and* recorded as `policy.floor.rejected` in the audit chain first - because
the error response is seen only by the person who tried, and "somebody tried
to make rollbacks auto-execute" is exactly what a security review looks for.

An open incident on this application requires `confirm_active_incident`, and
a confirmed mid-incident edit invalidates approvals granted under the
previous version rather than silently re-interpreting them.

What a candidate document would do, evaluated by the engine that decides.

Same code path as a real decision, so "what would this change" and "what
does this do" cannot diverge. A candidate the floor refuses comes back with
`accepted: false` and the rule that refused it, rather than as an error - the
editor has to show it beside the current decisions.

get.description:
Every version, newest first, each naming its author.

`read_audit` rather than `edit_policies`: the Auditor's whole job is to read
what changed and who changed it, and an audit trail only the editor can see
is not an audit trail.

post.description:
Everything at once: every connector tested in its own direction, every
journey probe run in every declared region, and the readiness score
recomputed from what came back.

One handshake's worth of credential for the caller's own session (REQ-033).

A write with no permission, and the third of its kind after logout and the
war room's four. It carries none for the same reason: the frozen roles matrix
gives `Role.SME` nothing, and the SME is the person whose pager this socket
feeds - a permission here would disconnect exactly the people an incident
exists to reach. The control that replaces it is that the route has no
parameter at all: the ticket is cut from the principal the request already
resolved, so a caller cannot ask for one naming anybody else's session, user
or tenant.

It is a write rather than a read because redeeming it consumes it, so issuing
one changes server state - and because a GET returning a credential is a
credential in a browser history.

get.description:
The live transcript. Says so plainly when no bridge is bound rather than
rendering an empty panel that looks like silence.

post.description:
Say something. Self-scoped: the author is the session and cannot be
anybody else, and speaking marks you present in the room.

get.description:
What somebody walking in at minute forty needs to know.

Addressed to the caller when they are in the room: what is being asked of
*them* is the part a responder reads first. `source` says who wrote it -
`template` today, `model` when S5's writer lands.

post.description:
Close an incident. Terminal: a regression afterwards is a new declaration
by a person at a new time, which is what the record should say.

get.description:
The board, having first checked whether anything on it has stopped being
true.

The contradiction sweep runs on read as well as on the bus: a contradiction
that only appeared after a background job would let somebody open the screen
and see a statement the platform already knew was wrong.

post.description:
Write a draft, grounded on this incident's graph nodes.

A draft, always. There is no parameter that issues one, and the audience's
approval permission is checked when somebody approves it - not here, because
drafting is the part a paged SME should be able to do.

A named person with the audience's permission says the text is right.

The permission is not on the route because the *audience* decides which one
applies and the route has not read the communication yet. It is enforced in
the service, against the audience, with `approve_customer_comms` for anything
customer-facing and `approve_exec_comms` for leadership.

A new draft carrying a redline against what was published.

The issued text is never edited. The redline is computed from the two bodies
rather than typed, so a correction cannot claim to change one thing while
changing another, and it needs its own approval like any other communication.

Publish. A person, always - there is no scheduler behind this route and no
configuration that could add one.

get.description:
Every attempt to change this application's estate during this incident.

`retry_blocked` travels beside `state`: a client must not offer retry on an
uncertain outcome, because the target may have applied it after SignalForge
stopped waiting.

post.description:
Ask for an action. The one entry point to every consequential call.

Arguments are validated against the schema the application published, the
policy engine decides, and the decision is recorded with its `rules_hit`
before anything happens. A high-risk action returns `approval_required` and
creates the approval request; asking for `intent: auto` on one returns a
recorded BLOCK naming the floor rule.

A person holding approve_high_risk says yes, for a bounded time.

The approval is bound to this execution and to a fingerprint over the action,
its arguments, its risk class and the policy version - so it authorises this
request and nothing else, and it stops authorising anything the moment any of
those change.

Undo what landed, through the action's declared reverse action.

A compensation is a full execution in its own right and goes through the same
policy decision and approval gate: undoing a failover is as consequential as
doing one.

Ask the target system what actually happened.

The only door out of `uncertain`. Resolves to `completed_late` (do not
repeat), `not_applied` (a retry is safe) or `partial` (compensate, continue
or take over), and only `not_applied` clears `retry_blocked`.

A fresh attempt at something that provably did not happen.

Refused with 409 while the previous outcome is unknown, and the refusal is
audited: retrying an unreconciled rollback is exactly the moment this control
exists for.

Withdraw an approval that has not been spent. Saying no later has to be
as easy as saying yes was.

Send an approved execution.

Everything is re-checked here and nothing is trusted from the request that
created the row: the policy version in force now, the approval's expiry, the
fingerprint, and whether the approver still holds the permission. The
arguments sent are the ones the execution was authorised for, read back off
the ledger; a body is needed only when a value was redacted on the way in.

A person is doing the rest by hand, and says what they are doing.

The honest terminal state for an execution the platform cannot resolve. The
note is required: "a human took over" with no record of what they did is
worse than no state at all.

Try the ITSM again now instead of waiting for the retry sweep. Reconciles
before it creates, so a link left uncertain by a timeout cannot become a
second ticket.

get.description: The ack board, oldest first, each row carrying its own countdown.

post.description:
Page somebody who was not in the blast radius.

Command work: putting a phone call into somebody's night is a decision about
another person's time, so it carries `declare_incident`.

"I have this."

Self-scoped and carries no permission, because the role that answers a page
holds none. The control is that the page names its recipient and the session
names itself: acknowledging anybody else's page is a 403 from the entity,
whatever the caller's roles say. Idempotent and terminal.

Escalate now rather than waiting out the countdown.

Returns the *successor* page - the one now ringing - because that is the row
the board needs to start counting down.

get.description:
The same document, regenerated.

A PIR is derived, not stored: regenerating it from the record is the whole
guarantee, and a stored copy would be the thing that drifts.

post.description:
Generate the post-incident review from the incident's own records.

409 when the audit chain does not verify. A PIR is the artefact people quote
six months later, so it is not produced at all from records that no longer
match their hashes.

get.description: Plan versions, newest first. The diff triad reads the top two.

schema.title: Response Get Plans Incidents  Incident Id  Plan Get

post.description:
Write plan version n+1, marking every action kept, paused or added.

Never a replacement. The previous version stays readable and the assumption
that changed travels with the new one.

get.description:
Reconstruct the incident from the hash-chained audit log.

Returns a document whether or not the chain verifies, and says which it is.
Hiding a broken chain would be the one unforgivable behaviour here; refusing
to return anything would deny an auditor the very view that shows what was
tampered with.

patch.description:
Re-grade an open incident. Nothing else in the platform can: detection
proposes a severity and never sets one.

post.description: Move an incident to recovering, or back to active after a regression.

get.description: Commitments with an owner and a due time, harvested or typed.

post.description: Put work on the board. Command work, so it carries a permission.

patch.description: Reassign, re-time or cancel - all decisions about somebody else's work.

post.description:
Tick your own task.

Self-scoped: an owned task is completed by its owner and nobody else, because
"done" is a claim about work somebody did. An *unassigned* task is completable
by anybody in the tenant - somebody has to be able to close out work that was
actually done, and refusing until a commander assigns it first is how a board
fills with things everybody knows are finished.

get.description:
The four layers, the stability window and whether closure is locked.

Every check names the system it was read from, and none of them is the
Incident Brain: recovery is checked against the application, never against
the platform's own reasoning about it.

post.description:
Run one validation cycle against the application.

A cycle that does not confirm recovery writes its failure into the incident
graph as evidence, returns the incident to `active` if it was `recovering`,
increments the failed-cycle count and escalates after the number of cycles
this application's policy allows.

get.description:
The room: who should be there, who was paged, who turned up, and the
roles nobody holds.

Readable by every member of the tenant, on the same reasoning the incident
reads carry no permission (DR-071): a war room that the paged SME cannot open
is a war room that has failed at the one thing it exists for.

post.description:
Turn up. Self-scoped: you join yourself, into a room in your own tenant.

There is no field for joining somebody else, so there is nothing a
permission would protect that the session does not already decide.

post.description:
Issue a successor. Both keys stay live, each with its own secret, until
the old one is revoked - a sender cannot be switched atomically, because it
is a configuration change in somebody else's system.

get.description:
What is on this person's phone. The S22 mobile paging page reads this.

Self-scoped by construction: the recipient is the session and there is no
parameter for anybody else, which is what lets it carry no permission.

tags.description: The incident lifecycle: steady, watch and proposed are detection's stances; active, recovering and closed are an incident, and only a person moves between the two halves. Reads are session-scoped to the caller's tenant and carry no permission, because the frozen roles matrix gives the SME - the role that answers a page - none; every write names declare_incident, change_severity or close_incident. Also the change window: a deployment announced as started and never announced as completed.
tags.name: incidents

tags.description: Reconstructing a closed incident from the hash-chained record, and the post-incident review generated from it. Read-only and behind read_audit, which is the Auditor role's only permission. The tenant comes from the session and appears in no parameter, so a cross-tenant replay is not a check that could be got wrong. A replay reports whether the chain still verifies and names the first record that does not; the review refuses to generate at all when it does not, because a PIR is quoted.
tags.name: audit

tags.description: Ingest keys, and the five frozen push endpoints a sending application posts to.
tags.name: ingest

tags.description: The room an incident is run from: membership derived from the blast radius, paging with per-row acknowledgement countdowns and next-in-rotation escalation, the join brief, the live bridge and the task board. Four writes here carry no permission and are self-scoped instead - acknowledging, joining, speaking and completing your own task - because the frozen roles matrix gives the SME none, and the entity refusing to act on anybody else's behalf is a tighter control than a permission any holder could use on anybody's page.
tags.name: war-room

tags.description: What the platform believes about an incident and why: a versioned graph of facts, assumptions, evidence, impact, risks and hypotheses, each carrying provenance and each kept forever - nothing is deleted, and a revised belief supersedes rather than overwrites. Hypothesis confidence is computed here from weighted evidence and is never written by a model; the model writes the sentence beside it. Impacts publish `confirmed` (measured) and `predicted` (inferred from dependencies) as separate values and separate lists, because a predicted downstream outage read as an observed one is how a war room pages four teams for an outage that never happened. The copilot answers only from this incident's own graph and every citation must resolve to a node the retrieval returned; an answer that cites anything else is discarded rather than shown. These routes carry no permission, on the same reasoning the war room's reads carry none, and none of them can change incident state, execute an action or approve anything - there is no such path from here.
tags.name: incident-brain

tags.description: The consequential-action boundary: policy, the Tool Gateway, the execution ledger, next best action, communications and layered validation. Every call that changes an integrated system passes through one door and produces an explicit decision - `allow`, `approval_required` or `block` - carrying the ordered `rules_hit` that produced it and naming, per rule, whether it came from the hardcoded platform floor or the application's own policy. The floor is code, not configuration: the six high-risk classes (rollback, restart, failover, traffic shift, config change, customer-impacting) can never auto-execute, a read-only classification can never be given to something that mutates, an approval expires within an hour, and audit is not a field, so it cannot be switched off. A policy document contradicting any of that is refused with the rule that refused it and the attempt is written to the audit chain. An approval is bound to a fingerprint over the action, its arguments, its risk class and the policy version, and is re-checked at execution for expiry, spend, revocation, fingerprint and whether the approver still holds the permission. A timeout is `uncertain`, never failed: `retry_blocked` is set and the only move out is `reconcile`, which asks the target system what actually happened. Duplicate submits return the existing execution and send nothing. Next-best-action scores are arithmetic the server computes before any model is called; a model may write the sentence beside a score and can never change one. No route here sends a communication, closes an incident or executes without the decision chain above - there is no such path.
tags.name: governance
